images.caption: St Dogmael's Abbey. The present parish church is a modern structure, built within the precincts of the former abbey of St. Dogmael's, and probably out of much of its remains. Beyond two oak chairs, bearing dates 1700 and 1738 respectively, no furniture or fittings that may have belonged to any earlier edifice have been preserved...The ruins of the Abbey of St. Mary the Virgin, founded 1115 for monks of the reformed Benedictine Order of Tiron, stand south of the parish churchyard, from which they are separated by a wall.

images.caption: Crypt - St Dogmael's abbey The ornaments indicate that this wasn't just some damp cellar but part of the crypt of the abbey, where anything the monks would have treasured was stored.
images.alt: Crypt - St Dogmael's abbey The ornaments indicate that this wasn't just some damp cellar but part of the crypt of the abbey, where anything the monks would have treasured was stored.

images.caption: Kitchen - St Dogmael's abbey. This area in the SW corner of the complex must have been the kitchen of the abbey.  The remains of the walls suggest that there were two stone ovens next to each other (one pictured here).  These would have been surrounded by other rooms, presumably to utilise the heat generated for heating as well as cooking.  In the foreground, the official tour guide (661255).

images.filename: Medieval floor tiling - St Dogmael's abbey - geograph.org.uk - 661245.jpg
images.caption: Medieval floor tiling - St Dogmael's abbey. A patch of original floor tiles still persists in the abbey ruins despite having been exposed to the weather for centuries.  I'm not sure the technique used is the same as at Strata Florida (652905), but they do look similar.
images.alt: Medieval floor tiling - St Dogmael's abbey. A patch of original floor tiles still persists in the abbey ruins despite having been exposed to the weather for centuries.  I'm not sure the technique used is the same as at Strata Florida (652905), but they do look similar.

images.caption: St Dogmael's tour guide. Despite the name of the abbey, St Dogmaels, they've employed a cat as official tour guide.  After having returned some other visitors to the exit, the guide sat posing on this wall until I'd taken its picture and then showed us round the whole abbey, pointing out places of particular interest such as the medieval water supplies (661265), ovens (661273) and the church itself (309699).  Then it led us back to the entrance and went back - no doubt ready for the next customers!

images.filename: Water duct - St Dogmael's abbey - geograph.org.uk - 661265.jpg
images.caption: Water duct - St Dogmael's abbey. The monks have channelled a stream to flow underground through the abbey.  Here, at the top of the complex, this would have been fresh water supply, but further downstream, it is likely that the stream would have been used as a drain.  Pictured to the left of the duct is the official tour guide (661255).
